title: Policy
description: The one provider-neutral policy, .ai/repo/policy.yaml: budgets, verification, retention, enforcement and projections.

session.description: What the provider's episode events do beyond drawing the boundary: how much the start event hands the worker, and whether the compaction and end events record anything.

briefing_on_start.description: Hand the worker a briefing on the start event's standard output, which the provider adds to the context it is about to build. False restores the older silence, in which a continuation record is written and nothing loads it.

briefing_budget_lines.description: Hard cap on what the start event writes to the provider's context. Text that arrives in every episode is paid for in every episode.

checkpoint_on_compact.description: Record a derived checkpoint when the provider announces a compaction, and again when an episode closes. Both are moments at which what the episode knows stops being reachable. Neither asks whether a task is open: a checkpoint is the episode's record and a task is an optional relation it names when it has one (ADR 0052).

handover_on_end.description: Write a derived continuation record when an episode ends. Until ADR 0052 this happened only while a task was still active, so a repository whose last task had been handed over stopped writing the one record a future worker resumes from.

handover_on_fill.description: Install the provider mod that asks the worker for a continuation record when the context window nears its fill line, while there is still room for the writing turn. PreCompact derives a checkpoint because the worker cannot be asked at that moment; this asks before it. `capture install` converges on the value: only true installs it, and anything else removes a mod it wrote. Absent means off, because the mod writes into the adopter's own .claude/ tree and an absent key is not consent to that; the skeleton declares true (ADR 0123).

knowledge_on_end.description: Derive the knowledge an episode produced into candidate records under the tracked knowledge section as the episode closes, on every close path: the ledger lines it stamped are the evidence, and they are about to stop being reachable. Deterministic and without a model; a second run over the same evidence writes nothing (ADR 0091). Absent means on.

knowledge_on_compact.description: Derive the same records when the provider announces a compaction, which discards the conversation while the work continues, so the record exists whether or not the episode ever closes cleanly. Independent of checkpoint_on_compact: the two record different things. Absent means on.

stranded_after.description: How long an open episode may go without a sign of life before `majordomus recover` may close it. The sign of life is the later of the episode's own started_at and the newest ledger line it stamped. Generous on purpose: closing a live episode costs the worker inside it the boundary of its work, and leaving a dead one open another hour costs nothing.

ensure_server_on_start.description: On the start event, make sure the repository's shared server serves this checkout (`majordomus serve ensure`): a server is started when none answers, never built, and the briefing names where it stands. False leaves the server to the first MCP client.

freshness.description: How old a continuation record may be before it stops being current. This is a different question from divergence (exact/advanced/diverged/different_context), which says where the record's commit sits relative to HEAD and nothing whatever about time: a record is `advanced` on the day it is written and still `advanced` a month later. Declared once here and read by every surface; a second copy of either number in a shell function, a Rust constant or a page of prose is the drift this file exists to prevent.

fresh_minutes.description: Below this age a record is `fresh`: current, act on it.

stale_minutes.description: At or beyond this age a record is `stale`: history, never presented as the current instruction. Between the two it is `aging` — still current, but its age is stated.

record_sections.description: The sections a closed episode's record carries in its body, in order. The front matter is what a machine can prove; these are what the episode was for and how it turned out, composed from the worker's own checkpoints and decisions where it left any and from git and the ledger where it did not. A section named here with no writer in lib/derive.sh ends `session close` with exit 10 naming the section, so an unwritable section is a configuration error rather than a silently empty heading.

commit_record_on_end.description: Commit the record the end event publishes. Every surface that reads session records reads the tracked tree, so a record left in the working tree is written, validated, counted healthy and invisible. The commit carries that one path and runs no commit hook. False restores the older behaviour, in which the lifecycle wrote a record and nothing committed it.

push_record_on_end.description: Publish the record commit, as a fast-forward only and through the pre-push hook like any other push. That hook asks whether the task may be published, so the push often will not go out and the record travels with the worker's next push instead.

prompts.description: Bounds on the raw prompt archive under .ai/local/prompts/. Pruning replaces a prompt body with a tombstone and keeps every other field, including the provenance of its episode link; a record is never deleted. Either bound alone is a bound.

retention_max_days.description: A prompt body older than this many days is pruned.

retention_max_bytes.description: The total size of the prompt bodies the archive keeps; the oldest are pruned first past it.

knowledge.description: Bounds on the review queue of derived knowledge records under the tracked knowledge section. A candidate is a record the deriver wrote and nobody has judged; the queue is measured, never emptied by a machine, and both numbers are declared once here and read by the shell validator and the Rust reader alike (ADR 0091).

candidates_max_files.description: More records with status candidate than this awaiting review is an advisory doctor finding that names them: a review queue that grows without bound is a queue nobody reviews.

candidate_max_age_minutes.description: A candidate waiting longer than this since it entered the queue is an advisory doctor finding: it was not reviewed, it was ignored. The age is measured from the derivation that wrote the file, else the commit that added it, else the record's own date.

commit.description: What a commit message is held to. The type vocabulary is not here: it is the changelog's own, and a second copy under this key is the duplication the commit subsystem exists to remove.

subject_max_chars.description: The widest a subject line may be, measured whole including the type and scope.

scope_unknown.description: A scope outside the vocabulary the repository's own history yields.

fix_requires_test.description: A `fix` whose files include no test.

reference_unresolved.description: A record id in the message that the layer does not hold.

breaking_unexplained.description: A commit marked breaking with no body and no BREAKING CHANGE trailer.

intent.description: Whether work must be bound to what it serves before it starts, and the exemption classes a worker may give instead (ADR 0111). Absent is off: a policy that predates the block starts work as it always did.

binding.description: off: the binding is asked only when start is given --issue, --intent or --exempt. advisory: every start asks and a refused binding is reported. required: a refused or unreadable binding does not start, and plan start refuses an issue whose binding is refused.

exemptions.description: The classes a worker may give with a reason when the work serves no intent on purpose. The absence of an intent is never an exemption by itself.

benchmark.description: How majordomus bench samples, and the thresholds bench --check and the command budgets apply.

doctor_ms.description: Wall-time budget for `majordomus doctor`; over it the command WARNs and still exits on its findings.

watch_ms.description: Wall-time budget for `majordomus watch`; over it the command WARNs and still exits on its findings.

enter_ms.description: Wall-time budget for entering the repository (`majordomus env enter`) when a server is already serving this checkout, which is every entry but the first. Entering a directory is something a person does dozens of times a day and never chose to wait for.

enter_cold_ms.description: Wall-time budget for the first entry, which additionally finds that nothing answers and starts a server — and then returns, because entry never waits for a server it started to become ready.

use_cases.description: How use-case coverage is gated: per class of target, whether a gap fails, is reported, or is not looked at.

server.description: The shared server of a checkout, and the lease that decides which process owns it. These are the timings a lease contest is judged by; they were compiled constants until they were declared here.

probe_timeout_seconds.description: How long a probe waits for the current owner to answer before that silence counts as evidence. Too low and a live but slow owner is judged stale and taken over while it is still serving; too high and a wedged one holds the checkout's server for that long.

bind_grace_seconds.description: How long a lease that names no URL yet is left alone. A server writes its lease before it can serve, so a fresh lease without a URL is a starting owner rather than a dead one.

join_timeout_seconds.description: How long a process waits to join or create the lease file before it refuses rather than waiting forever.

busy_grace_seconds.description: How long a live owner that does not answer its probe is waited on, and asked again, before its lease is taken over. A probe that times out is not a dead server; a live process that stays silent this long is treated as wedged and replaced.

read_deadline_seconds.description: How long the shared server lets a connection go without a request read in full on it — waiting for a head, kept alive between requests, or reading a body — before it closes the connection and counts it in server.status. A connection whose request is being answered is never closed by it.
